title: Slaves and free Negroes at balls and theaters
summary: Slaves worked for wages, lived on their own and mixed with free Negroes at dances and the opera.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up under segregation: schools, neighborhoods, Jim Crow

blocks.x: What about Negroes? Did they have the free Negroes there or slaves?

Both. Both. They made a great many attempts to borrow the slave. But again, here's another thing that I guess you wouldn't find any place else in the United States, the whole state of a slave in a city like New Orleans. It's different and it's really not been studied yet. I've gotten only a sort of glimpse into it. But the outside of house servants, most the slaves here were skilled workers of one kind or another, and they worked for a wage. And the wage would be paid by anybody needing them, and their owner would then perhaps just take a monthly stipend from the slave. Say, if the slave earned 80 dollars a month, he might turn over 10 dollars a month to his owner. And it was on that basis that his owner might have invested in him. He might actually buy a slave knowing that he had a certain earning power. And his work more often than not necessitated that the slave live on his own, paying his own room and board. And that meant that his hours were free outside of his working hours. And since the city had so many free Negroes anyway, it was pretty hard to tell on the street who was a slave and who was a free Negro. And the free Negroes having their own dances for themselves, that is, I'm trying to distinguish those from the so-called quadrant balls or mixed dances, which were very abundant. The free Negroes would have dances and they couldn't tell whether there were slaves there or not. On one occasion, the police raided such a dance after a fight and they arrested 75 males. And when they registered them, it was found that 50 out of the 75 were in fact slaves all at this free Negro ball. And at the theaters, even though promises were made to the free Negroes who had a section in the balcony reserved for them, or in the French, in the Orleans area, a whole balcony reserved for them, the management promised often that they would make every effort to keep slaves up, that no slaves would come in. But again, how could you really tell? It's true that the slave was supposed to have a pass from his master to be on the streets like that, but the businessman at the door is not about to turn away a paying customer for lack of a pass. So if the slaves did get a chance to attend these operas and other musical functions, I don't know in what number, nobody will ever know that.
Well, would the free Negro have to carry any papers identifying in that side?

He had to have papers that would show that, or at least it would be advisable for him to have his papers of freedom on them all the time. However, New Orleans was not like a lot of the rest of the South, at least up until the 1850s, and I mean, did it even begin to crack down. It was a much more tolerant, lenient city. The Negroes of the city had a society of some sort that they called the Philharmonic Society prior to the Civil War, and I've even seen the tantalizing indications that possibly white musicians played in society with them on occasion, but I haven't been able to pin that down yet. There are hints to this effect. They had, for a brief time, they had their own theater, and they had their own theater, which they hoped to put on opera, and they did put on vaudeville, although apparently it wasn't a very long-term success. But they were always in the musical stream of New Orleans as much as anybody else was, Negro and Slate. What about, it just occurred to me,
